intro: So you're the one who's been bending rules around the neighborhood. Word gets around. I'm Pablo.
Out front I sell luggage. I have never sold a suitcase. Back here, I solve problems. People's problems become my problems, and my problems become your opportunities.
Three jobs a day. You pick how you do them. Do them clean, the 114½ never hears your name. Do them sloppy, Sgt. Bev learns how to spell it.
One more thing: we don't hurt anybody here. This is a business. Badly run, but a business.

Errand Kid: The kid's back. Sit. Don't touch the suitcases, they're load-bearing.
You want work? Everybody starts at the bottom. The bottom is very busy today.
Corner Regular: Ah, my regular. The corner speaks well of you. The corner speaks a lot.
People on Steinway know your face now. That's good. Also bad. Mostly good.
Known Face: Look who it is. Sal at the deli asked about you. I told him you're in luggage.
You're a known face now. Keep the face. Lose the habit of using your real name.
Pablo's Guy: My guy! Sit, sit. I saved you the good chair. It has all four legs.
When people ask who handles things, I say you. Don't make me a liar. I'm already a notary.
Street Legend: A legend in my back room. My mother would be proud. She'd also be confused.
They tell stories about you on 30th Avenue. Some are true. Let's keep it that way.

pablo.halo: Pablo took his cut first. "You've got a churchgoer's face. I pay faces like that less until they prove me wrong."
pablo.refuse: "Not today. You're hot. You glow. Sgt. Bev could find you in the dark. Go lay low a day or two."
pablo.holding: Pablo's phone goes straight to voicemail. "You've reached Pablo's Discount Luggage. If you're calling from the 114½, wrong number."
pablo.lawyer: Whitlock & Hale LLP: we never ask what you did. We bill for not asking.

crew.name: Tito
lines: The van has two speeds: parked and late. Today it's parked.
I know every alley between here and the Bronx. I've named four of them.
Pablo says drive careful. I say the potholes drive me.
crew.cover: Tito told the 114½ he was driving alone, "for the vibes." Sgt. Bev believed him. Nobody knows why.

crew.name: Gigi
lines: I keep Pablo's books in pencil. Pencil forgives.
Every number tells a story. I prefer short stories.
Receipts are for people who plan to get caught.
crew.cover: Gigi produced a ledger proving you were at a bingo night in Bayside. It had a coffee stain. Very convincing.

crew.name: Auntie Bee
lines: I've known Sgt. Bev since she was a crossing guard. She still owes me a casserole dish.
Everybody on this block owes me something. Mostly casserole dishes.
Sit, eat, then we talk business. In that order.
crew.cover: Auntie Bee walked into the 114½ with a tray of baklava and walked out with your name off the report.

table.title: Pablo's Thursday table
table.blurb: Once a week Pablo's bigger guests sit down for cards, and nobody plays for the cards. Favors change hands. You leave with something.
table.locked: A curtain, a card table, and voices you'd swear were on the news. "Thursday table's for Hustlers," says Pablo. "Bend a few more rules and pull up a chair."
wins: A city inspector owed a florist who owed a developer who owed Pablo. You were the last link.
You folded three hands on purpose. A man in a fleece vest remembered it and paid you for your manners.
Somebody's cousin needed a parking permit. Somebody else had one. You were the handshake in the middle.
Auntie Bee won every hand and gave you a cut for "keeping the tea hot."

jobs.title: Pablo has forty pairs of designer sneakers with the logo printed upside down. Someone has to sell them on Steinway.

options.label: Sell them as the real thing
options.win: "Limited edition," you said. "Upside down is the point." Thirty-one pairs gone by lunch.
options.fizzle: A teenager turned the shoe over, laughed at you, and filmed it. Nobody bought a thing.

options.label: Sell them as "inspired by"
options.win: "Inspired by," you said, like a museum. People respect honesty in a knockoff.
options.fizzle: Turns out nobody is inspired by anything on a Tuesday.

jobs.bust: A man in a windbreaker asked for a size 10, then showed you a badge. It was a real badge. The shoes were not real shoes.
jobs.caught: Remember the upside-down sneakers? A buyer's mom took a pair to the 114½. Sgt. Bev wore them to work while she wrote you up.
jobs.headline: Steinway shoe sale ends badly: {name} tells police the logo was "a design choice."

jobs.title: A laptop "fell off a delivery bike." Pablo needs someone to find it a new home before the owner finds the old one.

options.label: Sell it to the guy at the pawnshop
options.win: The pawnshop guy didn't ask. You didn't tell. A beautiful relationship.
options.fizzle: The pawnshop guy opened the lid. The lock screen said REWARD IF FOUND with a number. He slid it back to you.

options.label: Wipe it and sell it online
options.win: Factory reset, a good photo, "barely used." Technically true.
options.fizzle: It wanted a password to reset. You tried "password." It was not password.

jobs.bust: The laptop's location tracker led the owner, a very calm accountant and two officers right to you.
jobs.caught: Remember the laptop that fell off a bike? Its owner turned on the tracker. It led the 114½ to the pawnshop, and the pawnshop led them to you.
jobs.headline: Laptop that "fell off a bike" lands {name} at the 114½. The bike could not be reached for comment.

jobs.title: Lunaria's show is sold out. Pablo has a stack of tickets of "varying realness." Work the line outside.

options.label: Sell the whole stack, real or not
options.win: Every ticket gone in twenty minutes. Some of them will even scan.
options.fizzle: The fans had been burned before. They checked every ticket against a flashlight. You sold none.

options.label: Only sell the real ones, at a markup
options.win: Real tickets, unreal prices. Everybody cried, for different reasons.
options.fizzle: The venue released more seats at the door. Your markup lost to a box office.

jobs.bust: A fan's ticket bounced at the door. She pointed at you. Twelve fans and one security guard pointed at you.
jobs.caught: Remember Lunaria's show? A fan with a fake ticket posted your face. A thousand fans found you. So did the 114½.
jobs.headline: Lunaria fans identify ticket seller {name} in record time. "We stream, we don't forget."

jobs.title: A man pays cash to have a parking spot on 30th Avenue held with a lawn chair. All day. Against all comers.

options.label: Hold the spot like it's yours
options.win: Eleven drivers tried. Eleven drivers left. You and the lawn chair are a legend on 30th.
options.fizzle: A tow truck took the spot, the chair and nearly you.

options.label: Rent the spot out by the hour
options.win: Six cars, forty minutes each, cash only. The man came back to an empty spot and a chair.
options.fizzle: The man came back early. He took his chair and his money and gave you a look.

jobs.bust: A traffic agent wrote the chair a ticket. Then she wrote you one. Then she called it in, because she was bored.
jobs.caught: Remember the lawn chair? The 114½ found it, with your name on the back in marker. Who labels a lawn chair?
jobs.headline: 30th Avenue parking feud: {name} and a lawn chair cited together. The chair has a lawyer.

jobs.title: The Astoria Park hot-dog contest is Saturday. Pablo bet big on the guy from Ditmars. Make sure the guy from Ditmars wins.

options.label: Swap the rivals' buns for stale ones
options.win: The rivals chewed like they were eating a sofa. Ditmars won by nine dogs. Pablo wept.
options.fizzle: The rivals didn't eat the buns. They ate the hot dogs and threw the buns at the crowd. Ditmars lost.

options.label: Coach the guy from Ditmars
options.win: Water, rhythm, no fear. Ditmars ate forty-one and called his mother. You earned your cut.
options.fizzle: Ditmars got the hiccups at dog twelve. You can't coach hiccups.

jobs.bust: A judge saw you at the bun table holding a bag of very old bread. Contest security is two retirees, and they are fast.
jobs.caught: Remember the hot-dog contest? A runner-up sent the stale buns to a lab. The lab was his cousin. The cousin called the 114½.
jobs.headline: Hot-dog contest scandal: {name} linked to "Bungate." Astoria Park demands a rematch.

jobs.title: A diner wants 200 five-star reviews by Friday. Pablo has the accounts. He needs someone who can type like 200 different people.

options.label: Write all 200 reviews
options.win: "Best pancakes in Queens," you wrote, 200 ways. The diner is now 4.9 stars. The pancakes are a 3.
options.fizzle: You used the same typo in 60 reviews. The app deleted them all in an afternoon.

options.label: And one-star the diner across the street
options.win: Up goes one diner, down goes the other. Pablo calls it "market forces."
options.fizzle: The diner across the street has a grandson in tech. Every review got traced to one phone in one afternoon.

jobs.bust: The reviews all came from Pablo's Discount Luggage's Wi-Fi. The 114½ has a detective who reads reviews for fun.
jobs.caught: Remember the 200 reviews? The diner across the street hired someone to trace them. They traced them to you.
jobs.headline: 200 reviews, one author: {name} named in Astoria pancake review scandal.

jobs.title: Pablo's notary stamp is real. His notary license has been "pending since 2009." A stack of leases needs stamping.

options.label: Stamp the whole stack
options.cost: A lot of leases on thin ice
options.win: Stamp, stamp, stamp. Eighty leases "notarized." Your wrist hurts. Your bank doesn't.
options.fizzle: The stamp ran out of ink at lease four. Pablo had no more ink. Pablo never has more ink.

options.label: Read them first, stamp the clean ones
options.win: Half the leases were fine. Half had a clause about "the landlord's nephew." You stamped the fine half.
options.fizzle: None of them were clean. Not one. You stamped nothing and went home.

jobs.bust: A landlord brought a "notarized" lease to Queens Housing Court. The judge asked who the notary was. The lease said you.
jobs.caught: Remember the lease stamps? One ended up in Queens Housing Court. The judge has a long memory and a short temper.
jobs.headline: Housing Court asks: who notarized 80 leases with an expired stamp? The answer: {name}.

jobs.title: A van full of "surplus" designer handbags needs to get from the Bronx to Astoria before sunrise. Pablo says it's not stolen, "just extremely discounted."

options.label: Drive the van yourself
options.win: Bridge, highway, 31st Street, done by 5 a.m. The handbags are in Pablo's "luggage" now.
options.fizzle: The van wouldn't start. You spent the night in it with 300 handbags and no heat.

options.label: Pay a cousin to drive it
options.cost: Half the fee goes to the cousin
options.win: The cousin drove. You slept. The handbags arrived. Teamwork.
options.fizzle: The cousin took a wrong turn into New Jersey and came back with the van and a story.

jobs.bust: A bridge toll camera, a broken taillight and a cop who loves handbags. You never stood a chance.
jobs.caught: Remember the handbag van? A toll camera had a very clear picture of the driver. It was you, eating a bagel.
jobs.headline: Handbag van stopped on the bridge. Driver {name} insists it is "a mobile closet."

jobs.title: The block association raffle has a flat-screen TV for first prize. Pablo's cousin is going to win it. You're going to make sure.

options.label: Load the drum with his tickets
options.win: The cousin won. He acted surprised. He is a terrible actor. Nobody noticed.
options.fizzle: Mrs. Papadopoulos runs the drum. Mrs. Papadopoulos checks the drum. You put the tickets back.

options.label: Just sell him a lot of tickets
options.win: He bought 300 tickets. Of course he won. That's just math.
options.fizzle: He bought 300 tickets. A girl with one ticket won. That's also math.

jobs.bust: Mrs. Papadopoulos caught you with a fistful of tickets and a guilty face. She called the 114½. She has them on speed dial.
jobs.caught: Remember the block raffle? The cousin posted the flat-screen online with "thanks to my inside man." He tagged you.
jobs.headline: Block raffle rigged: the flat-screen goes back, and {name} goes to the 114½.

jobs.title: Pablo has one food-truck permit and four food trucks. The sticker has to move from truck to truck all day without an inspector noticing.

options.label: Run the sticker between trucks
options.get: A day's fee from four trucks
options.win: Eight swaps, four trucks, one sticker, no inspector. You are the fastest runner on Steinway.
options.fizzle: The sticker lost its stick at swap three. You held it on the window with your hand for an hour.

options.label: Keep it on one truck, close the rest
options.win: One legal truck, one long line, one very honest afternoon. Pablo called you "a coward with a future."
options.fizzle: It rained. Nobody bought tacos. Even legal tacos.

jobs.bust: The inspector photographed the same sticker on two trucks in the same minute. You were holding it.
jobs.caught: Remember the food-truck sticker? The inspector compared photos. Same sticker, four trucks, one runner: you.
jobs.headline: One permit, four food trucks: {name} fined in Steinway's sticker shuffle.

jobs.title: A gallery in Long Island City wants an "undiscovered early work" by a famous dead painter. Pablo has a guy and a hair dryer to age the paint.

options.label: Sell it to the gallery as real
options.win: The gallery owner cried. She called it "raw." The guy painted it Tuesday.
options.fizzle: The gallery owner sniffed it and said "hair dryer." She's been in the business a long time.

options.label: Sell it as a "tribute piece"
options.win: "A tribute," you said. The gallery hung it beside a sign that said "homage." Everybody won.
options.fizzle: Nobody wants a tribute. They want a scandal.

jobs.bust: The gallery's appraiser found a price sticker from a craft store under the paint.
jobs.caught: Remember the early masterpiece? An art critic X-rayed it and found a grocery list underneath. The 114½ has an art squad now. It's one guy.
jobs.headline: LIC gallery's "lost masterpiece" was painted last Tuesday. Seller: {name}.

jobs.title: The LUXURY CONDOS SOON lot needs a community meeting about the new tower. Pablo's client wants it held where nobody will hear about it.

options.label: Hold it in a basement at 7 a.m.
options.cost: The block never gets a say
options.win: Three people came. Two were the developer. The tower is "approved by the community."
options.fizzle: Ms. Abernathy from the block association heard. Ms. Abernathy hears everything. She brought forty people.

options.label: Post the flyers, in very small print
options.win: The flyers were up. Technically. Two millimeters tall. Nobody came. Legal.
options.fizzle: A man with a magnifying glass read every flyer. He is now running for City Council.

jobs.bust: Ms. Abernathy filmed the empty basement meeting and sent it to Lola Lowdown and the 114½ at the same time.
jobs.caught: Remember the secret community meeting? Ms. Abernathy found the sign-in sheet. Three names. Yours was one.
jobs.headline: Luxury condo "community meeting" held in a basement at dawn. Organizer: {name}.

jobs.title: City Hall needs 10,000 ribbons for the Mayor's ribbon-cuttings. Pablo's cousin makes ribbons. Sort of. Get the contract.

options.label: Take the clerk to a very long lunch
options.cost: A clerk's career if it comes out
options.win: Three courses, one handshake, 10,000 ribbons. Mayor Papa-Dani cut the first one live on Clout TV.
options.fizzle: The clerk ordered the lobster, thanked you, and gave the contract to a ribbon company with a website.

options.label: Put in a low bid, fair and square
options.cost: The cousin has to make real ribbons
options.win: Lowest bid, won fair. The cousin learned to make ribbons. The Mayor said they "cut like a dream."
options.fizzle: A company in Ohio bid one cent lower. Ohio wins again.

jobs.bust: The purchasing clerk's lunch receipt was on the city's expense report. With your name. Spelled right.
jobs.caught: Remember the ribbon contract? City Hall audited the lunch. The lobster was itemized. So were you.
jobs.headline: Ribbongate: {name} named in City Hall ribbon contract probe. The Mayor "has cut thousands and regrets none."

jobs.title: A billionaire's yacht off Astoria needs forty cases of "vintage" wine by tonight. The wine is from Tuesday. The labels are from 1961.

options.label: Deliver it with a straight face
options.win: The billionaire swirled, sniffed and said "you can taste the history." You can taste Tuesday.
options.fizzle: The yacht's sommelier opened one bottle and quietly asked you to leave the boat. By rowboat.

options.label: Tell him it's young and good
options.win: "Young and good," you said. He laughed, bought all forty cases and asked if you were single.
options.fizzle: He only drinks old wine. He only drinks old everything. Even his jokes.

jobs.bust: The harbor patrol stopped the delivery boat. One of the officers is a wine nerd. It was over in one sip.
jobs.caught: Remember the yacht wine? The billionaire hosted a tasting. A guest read the label's fine print: "bottled last week."
jobs.headline: Billionaire's "1961" wine was bottled this month. Delivered by: {name}.
